description: Autonomy policy. The classifier reads a diff and computes a FLOOR: the lowest tier this change may be handled at, given what it touches. It is not a verdict. The tier that applies is set by impact, by the quality of the evidence available, by reversibility and by what is unknown, and a receipt may declare a higher tier than the floor, never a lower one. That asymmetry is the whole mechanism: a machine cannot argue its own risk down, and a human can always argue it up.

T1.name: Agent authors, gates decide
T1.human_involvement: Review after merge, by sampling. No human is in the critical path.
T1.rationale: Blast radius is one screen. The gates that matter (build, regression suite, boundary rules) are mechanical and complete for this class.

agent_may.merge: on green, without a human in the path
agent_may.deploy: no, deployment is a separate decision

T1.escalates_when: the change carries a marker: money, tenant scope, authorisation, schema, or the test surface.

T2.name: Agent authors, human approves before merge
T2.human_involvement: Named reviewer approves the PR. The reviewer reads the receipt first, the diff second.
T2.rationale: Mechanical gates catch the shape of the change but not its intent. A human confirms the intent was the right one.

agent_may.merge: only after a named human approves

T3.name: Human decides, agent implements
T3.human_involvement: An engineer writes the approach in the ticket before any agent runs, approves the PR, and signs the named control (schema label, rollback note).
T3.rationale: The failure mode is silent and expensive: wrong rows, lost money, a lock held across a call. Tests can prove a change is wrong, not that it is right.

agent_may.modify: only what the approach written by an engineer describes
agent_may.merge: only after a named human approves and signs the named control

T4.name: No agent authorship
T4.human_involvement: An engineer authors the change. The agent is allowed to read, search, summarise and draft a design note, never to produce the diff that ships.
T4.rationale: The change alters the rules the rest of the system relies on. Reviewing it costs more than writing it.

agent_may.execute: build and the suites, to investigate

classes.title: UI and application development
classes.risk: Wrong rendering is visible, cheap to revert, and caught by a screen. The real risk is a view reaching past the presentation layer for data it was not given.
context_pack: harness/agent-instructions/CONVENTIONS.generated.md (mined from the tree, not written from memory)
The model, the view and the factory for the screen being changed, plus one sibling screen as a worked example
The localisation convention: user facing strings come from resources, never from literals in a view
The list of types the presentation layer may not reference (policy/boundaries.json)
classes.status_note: T-001 went through the full gate set as a T1.

classes.title: Database transactions
classes.risk: A read-then-write on stock or money without a transaction or a guard is correct in every test and wrong under two concurrent orders. The damage is silent and it is in the ledger.
context_pack: The service being changed, its interface, and its existing tests
The entity mapping and the current schema of every table the change reads or writes
The transaction and isolation convention actually in use in the surrounding code, quoted
The concurrency scenario the change must survive, written by the engineer, not inferred by the agent
classes.mapping_note: Stock is the second ledger of this platform and it is not kept under a folder called data. ProductService is listed by name because a path prefix cannot say 'the part of the catalogue that moves quantities'. Every policy of this kind ends up with a handful of named files; the ones here are listed rather than hidden behind a clever glob.
classes.status_note: T-002 and T-004 are the worked case: an invariant, a plausible change that breaks it, a correction.

classes.title: Performance
classes.risk: An agent optimises what it can see. Cache keys that forget a scope, and queries that move work into a loop, both pass every functional test.
context_pack: The measurement that motivated the change: query plan, timing, or row counts, taken before
The cache key convention and the invalidation path for the entity touched
The scopes every key must carry in this system (store, vendor, customer roles, language)
classes.detection_limit: Performance is the class this classifier detects worst. Cache keys and indexes are visible in a diff; a query moved inside a loop is not, and materialising a list is so common that a rule on it would fire on every change and be turned off within a week. The honest fix is not a cleverer regex: it is a query counter in the test harness, so a change that turns one query into forty fails on a number instead of on a pattern. That is scoped in docs/POINTING-IT-AT-YOUR-PLATFORM.md, and it is not implemented here.
classes.status_note: An index shipped with T-002 and no measurement was taken. The gate this class needs is a query counter, which is not built here.

classes.title: Integrations
classes.risk: The other side is not in the repository. Nothing in the build fails when the payload quietly changes shape, and the party that notices is the accounting system, a day later.
context_pack: The contract of the other side: the payload we send today, pinned as a fixture
The failure and retry convention used by the existing integrations here
Which fields are the other side's identity keys, and which of ours are scoped per tenant
classes.status_note: T-003 went through, including the attempt the boundary rule stopped.

classes.title: Concurrency
classes.risk: The failure appears under load, in production, once. An agent has no way to observe it and the suite has no way to reproduce it.
context_pack: The interleaving the change must survive, written as two ordered timelines
What the lock or the guard protects, and what is allowed to happen inside it
The existing concurrency primitives used in this area, quoted from the tree
classes.status_note: The reservation path is read then write with no transaction, and the harness does not reproduce the race. The guard narrows the damage; nothing here proves the race is closed. Reproducing it needs the real engine.

classes.title: Legacy architecture
classes.risk: Old code encodes decisions nobody restates. An agent reads the code and infers the rule from what it sees, which is how a fifteen year old exception becomes tomorrow's convention.
context_pack: The decision record for this area if one exists, and the explicit statement that none does if it does not
The list of callers, produced by search, not by memory
The boundary baseline: which exceptions to the rules already exist here and why they were kept
classes.status_note: No ticket in this repository touched it. The class is listed because the platform has the debt, not because the policy has been tried on it.

classes.title: Fundamental system changes
classes.risk: The change moves the ground other changes stand on: dependency registration, the startup pipeline, the data provider, the plugin contract. Review costs more than authorship.
context_pack: A design note written by an engineer, reviewed before any code exists
The migration and rollback plan for every environment
The agent's role in writing: none
classes.status_note: No ticket touched the engine or the data provider, by design.

markers.title: Schema change
markers.why: A migration runs once, on live data, in an order nobody replays. It is the one change where being wrong is not revertible by a revert.

markers.title: Money path
markers.why: The totals suite is the only artefact in the tree that states what the arithmetic is supposed to be.

markers.title: Tenant scope
markers.why: In a multi tenant platform, the dangerous query is not the one that fails, it is the one that returns another tenant's rows and looks fine.

markers.title: The tests themselves
markers.why: An agent that can change the tests can change what green means. Every other gate in this policy is downstream of this one, so a change that touches the control surface is never merged on a machine's word alone.

markers.title: Permissions and access
markers.why: A screen is not low risk because it is a screen. A change that alters who may do something is the same class of risk as a change to the ledger, and it arrives in presentation files.

markers.title: The harness itself
markers.why: The agent that runs a case does not get to edit its own referee in the same breath. Changing the rules, the tests of the rules or the workflow that runs them is a separate decision with its own label.

gate_definitions.receipt: tickets/<id>/receipt.md exists and carries every required section.
gate_definitions.classifier-agreement: The tier and classes written in the receipt equal the ones the classifier computes from the diff. An agent that under declares its own risk fails here.
gate_definitions.build: The upstream tree, with the patch applied, compiles.
gate_definitions.architecture: The boundary rules hold, measured against a recorded baseline. New violations fail, pre existing ones are listed and frozen.
gate_definitions.golden-behaviour: The selected upstream suites (orders, catalog, shipping, tax) pass on the patched tree.
gate_definitions.pinning-test: The patch adds or changes a test that fails without the change and passes with it.
gate_definitions.contract-test: The payload crossing the boundary is pinned by a fixture and compared byte for byte.
gate_definitions.measurement-in-receipt: The receipt carries a before and an after number, taken the same way.
gate_definitions.human-approval: A named human approved the pull request.
gate_definitions.schema-label: The pull request carries the human-review:schema label, applied by a human after reading the migration.
gate_definitions.rollback-note: The receipt states what running this migration backwards costs.
gate_definitions.design-note: A design note exists and was approved before the diff.
gate_definitions.harness-label: The pull request carries the harness-change label. Required for any change to the rules, their tests, or the workflow that runs them.

how_the_tier_is_decided.summary: Technical category is a prior, not an answer. A screen is not low risk because it is a screen: a screen that changes an amount, a permission or another tenant's rows is not a T1. That is what the markers are for, and they apply whatever folder the change is in.
axes: Impact: what is wrong in the world if this ships wrong. A rendered label, a wrong number in a ledger, another tenant's data.
Evidence: does a test exist that would fail. If the honest answer is no, the tier goes up until a human is in the path, or the ticket starts by building the evidence.
Reversibility: can this be undone by reverting the merge. A migration cannot. A payload already sent cannot.
Unknowns: anything the policy does not map, an area with no owner, a dependency nobody has read. An important unknown escalates rather than defaults.

criteria_for_an_erp.note: These are the questions to put to a change in a platform of this kind. They are criteria, not findings about any particular company.
criteria_for_an_erp.transactions_and_concurrency: Is the invariant written down. What happens if the work is interrupted half way. What happens if two of them run at once. Is the final state checked rather than the happy path. Is the application logic separated from what the database engine does, so a green suite on one engine is not read as a guarantee on another.
criteria_for_an_erp.tenant_isolation: Is there a negative test, with two tenants, that fails when a query forgets its scope. Do the background jobs, the caches and the exports carry the scope too, or only the request path.
criteria_for_an_erp.migrations_and_multiple_clients: Is the change compatible with the clients already deployed. Can it resume after a partial run. What does going backwards cost, and has anybody written that down before it runs.
criteria_for_an_erp.accounting_and_synchronisation: Duplicates, replays, out of order arrival, amounts, and whether the two sides can be reconciled after the fact.

how_the_tier_is_decided.per_tier_permissions: Each tier says separately what an agent may read, modify, execute, merge and deploy. Merging and deploying are never the same permission.
